scenes.tts: The first film followed ripples through one model river. How can scientists tell whether real blue and white catfish populations changed? They need the river's record, not one visit. Murky water hides fish from view.
scenes.caption: The first film followed ripples through one model river. How can scientists tell whether real blue and white catfish populations changed? They need the river's record, not one visit. Murky water hides fish from view.
scenes.visual: Rebuild the same 16:9 river cross-section and colour map from the first film: blue catfish BLUE, white catfish GOLD, prey TEAL, habitat GREEN, human pressures RED, labels WHITE. Water and marsh plants move continuously. A few fish pass, then fade behind a broad translucent brown 'murky water' band. The opening question appears while a magnifying glass searches the water and misses hidden fish.
scenes.narration: The first film followed ripples through one model river. How can scientists tell whether real blue and white catfish populations changed? They need the river's record, not one visit. Murky water hides fish from view.

scenes.visual: A boat glides into the same moving river. Overlay the title 'Reading the River's Record' for two seconds, then dissolve it while the boat keeps moving.

scenes.tts: Scientists from the Virginia Institute of Marine Science repeat bottom tows at many places. A boat pulls the same kind of net for a set time. The catch is sorted and counted. Repeating the method makes years more useful to compare.
scenes.caption: Scientists from the Virginia Institute of Marine Science repeat bottom tows at many places. A boat pulls the same kind of net for a set time. The catch is sorted and counted. Repeating the method makes years more useful to compare.
scenes.visual: The boat tows a large net along the bottom. A map inset fills the right third with several station dots lighting in sequence. The net lifts and transforms into two sorting tubs, BLUE and GOLD. Fish tally marks build beside each tub. A clock face and repeated-path arrow show a set method without displaying spoken numbers.
scenes.narration: Scientists from the Virginia Institute of Marine Science repeat bottom tows at many places. A boat pulls the same kind of net for a set time. The catch is sorted and counted. Repeating the method makes years more useful to compare.

scenes.tts: Those counts become a survey index for each fish. An index tracks how common that fish is in the surveyed area. It is not a count of every fish in the river. Think of it as a consistent signal from repeated samples.
scenes.caption: Those counts become a survey index for each fish. An index tracks how common that fish is in the surveyed area. It is not a count of every fish in the river. Think of it as a consistent signal from repeated samples.
scenes.visual: Tally marks from many station dots stream into a labelled block, 'survey calculation', then emerge as one BLUE point for one year. Repeat for GOLD. Keep a dotted river outline around the sampled area. A crossed-out whole-river fish counter appears only beside the phrase 'not a count', then clears.
scenes.narration: Those counts become a survey index for each fish. An index tracks how common that fish is in the surveyed area. It is not a count of every fish in the river. Think of it as a consistent signal from repeated samples.

scenes.tts: Keep blue catfish blue and white catfish gold, matching the first film. Build a separate trace for each fish across time. The two indexes use different math and river areas. Their heights cannot be compared directly with each other.
scenes.caption: Keep blue catfish blue and white catfish gold, matching the first film. Build a separate trace for each fish across time. The two indexes use different math and river areas. Their heights cannot be compared directly with each other.
scenes.visual: Transform the river into two large stacked graph panels that fill the frame. The upper panel is BLUE and the lower GOLD. Both are labelled 'survey index', with a bold divider reading 'separate scales'. Their vertical rulers slide apart to different sizes; a direct vertical comparison arrow fades away. Years appear as digits on screen only.
scenes.narration: Keep blue catfish blue and white catfish gold, matching the first film. Build a separate trace for each fish across time. The two indexes use different math and river areas. Their heights cannot be compared directly with each other.

scenes.tts: Now the full traces grow from left to right. The blue index rises from early zero catches, though it jumps between years. The white index is lower after its early high values. Each dot is one year inside a longer pattern.
scenes.caption: Now the full traces grow from left to right. The blue index rises from early zero catches, though it jumps between years. The white index is lower after its early high values. Each dot is one year inside a longer pattern.
scenes.visual: Plot the lesson's full computed data in the separate panels, with years spaced by actual time. BLUE points and connecting segments draw left to right; GOLD follows. Display the source values beside points as digits, never spoken. Mark the graphic 'computed from lesson table'. Do not smooth the lines or add a trend line.
scenes.narration: Now the full traces grow from left to right. The blue index rises from early zero catches, though it jumps between years. The white index is lower after its early high values. Each dot is one year inside a longer pattern.

scenes.tts: One blue point towers above nearby years. Should that single point settle the story, or should scientists use the full series? Make your prediction.
scenes.caption: One blue point towers above nearby years. Should that single point settle the story, or should scientists use the full series? Make your prediction.
scenes.visual: Keep both full traces visible. Enlarge the high BLUE point from the year shown as digits on screen and draw a question ring around it. The rest of the series dims but remains readable. Put the question across the center without covering either trace.
scenes.narration: One blue point towers above nearby years. Should that single point settle the story, or should scientists use the full series? Make your prediction.

scenes.visual: Deliberate predict pause. Hold the question and ringed BLUE point. Graph points pulse very slightly; no answer or verdict appears.

scenes.tts: Use the full series. One year can be unusually high or low. A zero also means none were caught in that survey, not that none lived anywhere in the river. The other years keep one point in context.
scenes.caption: Use the full series. One year can be unusually high or low. A zero also means none were caught in that survey, not that none lived anywhere in the river. The other years keep one point in context.
scenes.visual: Restore all points to full brightness and shrink the question ring. A bracket spans the entire time axis: 'use the full series'. At the early BLUE zeros, animate an empty net icon beside the label 'none caught in this survey'; fish silhouettes remain faint elsewhere in the river outline.
scenes.narration: Use the full series. One year can be unusually high or low. A zero also means none were caught in that survey, not that none lived anywhere in the river. The other years keep one point in context.

scenes.tts: Compare each fish with itself across time. The blue index became higher, while the white index stayed below its early high values. That opposite pattern shows that the surveyed river community changed. An index tracks change; it does not count every fish.
scenes.caption: Compare each fish with itself across time. The blue index became higher, while the white index stayed below its early high values. That opposite pattern shows that the surveyed river community changed. An index tracks change; it does not count every fish.
scenes.visual: In the BLUE panel, animate a broad left-to-right bracket labelled 'higher later'. In GOLD, add 'below its early highs'. Do not connect the panels with a causal arrow. The two brackets transform into a shared label, 'community pattern', while a whole-river counter stays crossed out.
scenes.narration: Compare each fish with itself across time. The blue index became higher, while the white index stayed below its early high values. That opposite pattern shows that the surveyed river community changed. An index tracks change; it does not count every fish.

scenes.tts: But a survey shows a pattern, not its cause. Shared prey makes competition one possible explanation. Pollution, habitat loss or other changes could also have affected white catfish. The graph alone cannot choose among those possibilities.
scenes.caption: But a survey shows a pattern, not its cause. Shared prey makes competition one possible explanation. Pollution, habitat loss or other changes could also have affected white catfish. The graph alone cannot choose among those possibilities.
scenes.visual: Slide the graphs left but keep them large. On the right, three equally weighted schematic paths appear: TEAL shared prey, RED runoff and a GREEN habitat patch shrinking. Each ends in a question mark beside the GOLD population, never in 'proved' or 'rejected'. A boundary line reads 'pattern ≠ cause'.
scenes.narration: But a survey shows a pattern, not its cause. Shared prey makes competition one possible explanation. Pollution, habitat loss or other changes could also have affected white catfish. The graph alone cannot choose among those possibilities.

scenes.tts: A careful claim has three parts. State the pattern, point to values from the same years, then explain a possible link. Keep may in the reasoning because the cause remains uncertain. That small word keeps the evidence honest.
scenes.caption: A careful claim has three parts. State the pattern, point to values from the same years, then explain a possible link. Keep may in the reasoning because the cause remains uncertain. That small word keeps the evidence honest.
scenes.visual: Transform the panels into three wide stacked blocks: 'CLAIM: pattern', 'EVIDENCE: same years', 'REASONING: may link'. Selected lesson values appear as digits inside the evidence block. The word 'may' grows larger in GOLD, then settles back into the reasoning sentence.
scenes.narration: A careful claim has three parts. State the pattern, point to values from the same years, then explain a possible link. Keep may in the reasoning because the cause remains uncertain. That small word keeps the evidence honest.

scenes.tts: The survey adds evidence to our river picture. When people change an ecosystem, populations may rise or fall. Evidence shows the pattern; further tests are needed to identify causes. Good science protects that line between observation and explanation.
scenes.caption: The survey adds evidence to our river picture. When people change an ecosystem, populations may rise or fall. Evidence shows the pattern; further tests are needed to identify causes. Good science protects that line between observation and explanation.
scenes.visual: Rebuild the original river behind the two separate traces. BLUE and GOLD fish swim under their matching graph panels. A solid bracket labels the observed 'pattern'; dotted question-mark arrows label possible 'causes'. The same colour-map legend from the first film remains at lower right.
scenes.narration: The survey adds evidence to our river picture. When people change an ecosystem, populations may rise or fall. Evidence shows the pattern; further tests are needed to identify causes. Good science protects that line between observation and explanation.
